title: The Milesians: Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes
subtitle: Three neighbors in one harbor city ask what everything is made of
objectives: Explain what the Milesians meant by the arche, or first principle, and why they looked for one
Describe the theories of Thales (water), Anaximander (the apeiron) and Anaximenes (air) and the reasons offered for each
Explain what made their explanations naturalistic and why that counts as an early form of scientific thinking
Understand how we know about these thinkers at all, given that almost none of their writings survive
Trace how each Milesian criticized and improved on the one before
hook:
Look around the room you are in. There is wood, glass, fabric, water in a cup, air you cannot see, perhaps a cat asleep on a chair. These things look and behave completely differently. A cup of water can become steam or ice. A log becomes ash and smoke. The cat ate food that somehow became cat.

Here is a startling thought: what if all of this, every last bit of it, is really one kind of stuff wearing different disguises? Today that idea sounds almost obvious, because we are told everything is made of atoms, or of particles, or of fields. But someone had to think it first. Around 600 BCE, three men living in the same Greek city, each probably knowing the others, proposed exactly that, and then argued with each other about what the one stuff was. Their answers were wrong. Their question was one of the most fruitful in history.

sections.heading: A Harbor City and a Detective Problem
sections.body:
Miletus sat on the western coast of Asia Minor, in modern Turkey. In the 6th century BCE it was one of the richest Greek cities in the world, a hub of shipping with dozens of colonies around the Black Sea and trading links to Egypt, Lydia and the Near East. As you saw on Day 1, this was exactly the kind of place where new ideas could take root. Its golden age ended in 494 BCE, when the Persians crushed a Greek revolt and sacked the city.

Before we meet its three famous thinkers, you need to know something uncomfortable: we have almost none of their own words. Thales may never have written a book at all. Anaximander and Anaximenes did write, but their books are lost. Everything we know comes from later authors who quoted, summarized or criticized them, sometimes centuries afterwards. The most important of these is **Aristotle** (384–322 BCE), who surveyed earlier thinkers in the first book of his *Metaphysics*. His student Theophrastus wrote a history of earlier opinions about nature, which itself is lost but was copied and excerpted by later writers. One of them, the 6th-century CE scholar Simplicius, preserved the only sentence of Anaximander we have.

These secondhand reports are called **doxography**, from the Greek for “writing down opinions.” Reading the earliest philosophers is therefore a bit like detective work. Aristotle, in particular, described his predecessors in his own vocabulary and through the lens of his own theories, so we always have to ask: is this what Thales thought, or what Aristotle thought Thales must have meant? Scholars refer to these early thinkers as the **Presocratics** (those before Socrates), and they still cite their fragments using a numbering system created by the German scholar Hermann Diels in 1903 and later revised by Walther Kranz.

sections.heading: Thales: Everything Is Water
sections.body:
**Thales** of Miletus (c. 624–c. 546 BCE) is traditionally called the first philosopher. Later Greeks counted him among the Seven Sages, a list of legendary wise men. Many stories cling to him, and you should hold them loosely:

- The historian Herodotus reports that Thales predicted a solar eclipse that halted a battle between the Lydians and the Medes. Astronomers date this eclipse to 585 BCE, which is why Thales is often dated by it. But many scholars doubt he could have predicted it with any precision; at most he may have used Babylonian cycles to say an eclipse was possible within a certain period.
- Plato tells of Thales falling into a well while gazing at the stars, mocked by a witty servant girl for wanting to know what was in the heavens while ignoring what was at his feet.
- Aristotle tells the opposite kind of story: that Thales used his knowledge of the weather to foresee a big olive harvest, rented all the olive presses cheaply, and made a fortune, proving philosophers could be rich if they cared to.

Both stories are probably legends, but together they show the two images of the philosopher that have stuck ever since: the absent-minded stargazer and the clever problem-solver.

What matters philosophically is Aristotle’s report that Thales said the **arche**, the origin or first principle of all things, is **water**. He also reportedly held that the Earth floats on water like a piece of wood. Why water? Aristotle admits he is guessing, but suggests Thales noticed that the nourishment of all things is moist, that heat itself seems to come from moisture, and that the seeds of all living things are wet. We might add that water is the one ordinary substance we routinely see as solid, liquid and vapor. If one thing could turn into everything, water is a reasonable first guess.

Aristotle also reports that Thales said the magnet has a soul because it moves iron, and that “all things are full of gods.” This shows Thales was no modern materialist. For him, the world seems to have been alive throughout, a view scholars call **hylozoism** (from *hyle*, matter, and *zoe*, life). The point is not that he dismissed the divine, but that he looked for the source of things inside nature itself rather than in a story about gods giving birth.

sections.heading: Anaximander: The Boundless
sections.body:
**Anaximander** (c. 610–c. 546 BCE) was younger than Thales and is described as his pupil or associate. He is credited with one of the first prose books in Greek, usually given the later title *On Nature*. And he saw a problem in his teacher’s theory.

The world is full of **opposites**: hot and cold, wet and dry, light and dark. Water is wet and cool. If everything came from water, how could fire, which is hot and dry, ever arise from it? Worse, if one of the opposites were the basic stuff, it would have overwhelmed and destroyed the others long ago. (Aristotle reports an argument along these lines in his *Physics*.) So Anaximander concluded that the source of everything cannot be any of the familiar stuffs. It must be something more basic, with no definite character of its own, from which the opposites separate out.

He called it the **apeiron**: the boundless, the unlimited, the indefinite. It is unlimited in amount, so it never runs out, and indefinite in kind, so it is not hot or cold or wet or dry. It is eternal and ageless, and later reports say he called it divine. From it, the opposites split off, and the world we know forms through their interaction.

Then comes the single sentence that survives, quoted by Simplicius. The things that exist come to be out of certain things and perish back into them, “according to necessity; for they pay penalty and retribution to each other for their injustice according to the assessment of Time.” Scholars argue about exactly which words are Anaximander’s and which are paraphrase, but the image is unforgettable. Nature is pictured as a courtroom. When summer heat dominates, it commits an “injustice” against cold, and must pay it back in winter. The world is governed not by the whims of gods but by a kind of **cosmic law**, a balance that keeps any one power from winning permanently.

This is a profound move. Anaximander explains something we can see (the regular cycle of seasons and the persistence of opposites) by appealing to something we cannot see (the apeiron and its lawful balance). Explaining the visible by the invisible, through a principle that applies everywhere, is what theoretical science still does.

sections.heading: Anaximander’s Daring Cosmos
sections.body:
Anaximander did not stop at first principles. He built an entire picture of the universe, and some of its features are astonishing for the 6th century BCE.

**The Earth hangs in space.** Thales had the Earth resting on water. But that invites an obvious question: what holds up the water? Anaximander’s answer was that nothing does. According to Aristotle’s *On the Heavens*, he argued that the Earth stays where it is because it sits at the center, at equal distances from everything, so it has no more reason to move in one direction than another. This is an argument from **symmetry**, and the philosopher Karl Popper called it one of the boldest ideas in the history of human thought. Anaximander pictured the Earth as a short cylinder, like a drum or a column section, with a depth one-third of its width. We live on the top face.

**The heavens as wheels of fire.** Later reports say he thought the Sun, Moon and stars were rings of fire enclosed in mist, visible through holes like the nozzle of a bellows. Eclipses happen when the holes become blocked. Wrong in detail, but notice that it is a mechanical model: nothing supernatural is required.

**The first map.** Later Greek geographers credited Anaximander with drawing the first map of the inhabited world. He is also credited with introducing the **gnomon**, a vertical rod whose shadow tracks the Sun, into Greece, though Herodotus says the Greeks learned of it from Babylon.

**The origin of humans.** Perhaps most remarkably, later sources report that Anaximander thought the first living creatures arose in moisture, and that humans must originally have developed inside fish-like creatures. His reasoning: human babies need a long period of care before they can feed themselves, so the very first humans could not have survived as helpless infants on their own. This is not Darwin’s theory of evolution, and we should not pretend it is. But it is a naturalistic argument about origins based on an observed fact about our species.

sections.heading: Anaximenes: Air and the Machinery of Change
sections.body:
**Anaximenes** (c. 585–c. 528 BCE), the youngest of the three, is said to have been Anaximander’s student. At first glance his theory looks like a step backward. Instead of the mysterious apeiron, he named an ordinary substance as the arche: **air** (in Greek *aer*, which could also mean mist or vapor).

But Anaximenes had a reason, and it was an important one. Anaximander had said the opposites “separate off” from the boundless, without explaining how. Anaximenes supplied a **mechanism**. Air, he said, changes by **rarefaction** (thinning out) and **condensation** (packing together). When air is rarefied, it becomes fire. When it is condensed, it becomes wind, then cloud, then water, then earth, then stones. Every kind of stuff is the same air at a different density.

This is a big conceptual advance. It explains differences of **quality** (fire versus stone) through differences of **quantity** (how tightly packed the air is). Modern physics does something similar when it explains the difference between ice, water and steam by how closely molecules are packed and how fast they move. Anaximenes even offered an everyday test. According to Plutarch, he pointed out that if you breathe on your hand with your mouth wide open, the breath feels warm, but if you blow through pursed lips, it feels cool, because compressed air is cold and loosened air is hot. (The real physics is different, involving expansion and mixing with room air, but the instinct to support a theory with a simple observation is exactly right.)

Why air? Air is everywhere, invisible yet powerful, and it is linked to life itself: we die when we stop breathing. A later report attributes to Anaximenes the thought that just as our soul, being air, holds us together, so breath and air surround the whole world. Scholars debate how much of that wording is genuinely his, but it suggests he saw a parallel between the living body and the cosmos. Like Thales, he also gave the Earth a support: it is flat and rides on air, like a leaf.

sections.heading: What the Milesians Started
sections.body:
Strip away the details, and the three Milesians share four commitments that would shape all later science and philosophy.

1. **The search for an arche.** Behind the dizzying variety of things there is an underlying unity. Aristotle used the word *arche* for this first principle; it can mean beginning, origin, source or ruling principle. The Milesians were looking for what everything comes from, what it is made of, and what it returns to.
2. **Naturalism.** Explanations should appeal to things within nature, such as water, air, condensation and balance, rather than to the personal decisions of gods. Aristotle called these thinkers *physiologoi*, students of **physis**, the Greek word for nature, from which we get “physics.”
3. **Generality.** A good explanation should cover many phenomena at once. Thales’ water was supposed to explain earthquakes, life and the stability of the Earth. One principle, many effects.
4. **Criticism.** Most strikingly, each thinker openly revised his predecessor’s view with reasons. Anaximander asked how water could produce fire. Anaximenes asked how the boundless produces anything. Popper argued that this “tradition of critical discussion” was the Greeks’ true invention: not any particular theory, but the habit of teachers encouraging students to find better answers.

The Milesians lacked much of what we now think of as science. They did not run controlled experiments, use precise measurements in their physical theories, or test predictions systematically. Their theories rested on observation, analogy and bold argument. That is why we call them proto-scientists, or the first scientific thinkers, rather than scientists in the modern sense.

The search for a single underlying stuff will be challenged almost at once. Pythagoras (Day 3) will suggest the deepest reality is not a stuff at all but **number** and structure. Heraclitus (Day 4) will put change itself at the center. And Parmenides (Day 5) will argue that the whole Milesian picture of one thing turning into many is logically impossible. The conversation has begun.

keyQuote.text: According to necessity; for they pay penalty and retribution to each other for their injustice according to the assessment of Time.
keyQuote.source: Anaximander, Fragment B1 (DK 12B1), as quoted by Simplicius

modernConnection.title: The Long Search for a Theory of Everything
modernConnection.body:
Physicists today are still, in a sense, Milesians. The dream of a **theory of everything**, a single framework from which all the forces and particles of nature could be derived, is a direct descendant of the search for the arche. Modern physics has already traveled far down that road. Thousands of chemical substances turned out to be combinations of about a hundred elements. The elements turned out to be arrangements of protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons and neutrons turned out to be made of quarks. In the Standard Model of particle physics, all of these are best described as excitations of underlying quantum fields. One stuff, many disguises.

Anaximenes’ insight that differences in quality come from differences in quantity is everywhere in science. The difference between a diamond and the graphite in your pencil is not a difference in what they are made of (both are pure carbon) but in how the atoms are arranged. The difference between ice and steam is how fast and how closely water molecules move.

The Milesian habit of criticism is also built into modern science. A research paper is supposed to be attacked by reviewers, rival labs try to replicate surprising results, and young scientists build careers by overturning their teachers’ theories. The physicist Carlo Rovelli, in his book on Anaximander, argues that this institutionalized disrespect for authority, combined with respect for evidence and argument, is the deepest legacy of Miletus.

But be honest about the differences. Modern physics earns its authority through mathematics and precise, testable predictions, such as the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, which theory and experiment match to many decimal places. The Milesians could not test their theories in anything like that way, and their guesses were often hopelessly wrong. There is also a deeper question they would recognize: even if we find the final equations, would that explain *why* there is something rather than nothing? A theory of everything might describe what the arche does without telling us why it exists at all. That leftover question is philosophy’s, not physics’.

vocabulary.definition: Greek for beginning, origin or ruling principle; the fundamental source or stuff from which everything comes and of which everything is made.
vocabulary.example: For Thales the arche was water; for Anaximenes it was air.

vocabulary.definition: Anaximander’s name for the first principle: the boundless or indefinite, unlimited in amount and having no definite qualities of its own.
vocabulary.example: Because the apeiron is neither hot nor cold, both heat and cold can emerge from it without one destroying the other.

vocabulary.definition: The approach of explaining events by causes found within nature rather than by the intentions of gods or supernatural forces.
vocabulary.example: Explaining thunder as clouds colliding rather than as Zeus’s anger is a naturalistic explanation.

vocabulary.definition: Greek for nature, especially the inner character or way of growing that makes a thing what it is; the root of the word physics.
vocabulary.example: Aristotle called the Milesians students of physis because they investigated the natural world.

vocabulary.definition: Anaximenes’ mechanism of change: air thins out to become fire, or packs together to become wind, cloud, water, earth and stone.
vocabulary.example: On Anaximenes’ view, a stone is simply air condensed to a very high degree.

vocabulary.definition: Ancient writing that collects and summarizes the opinions of earlier thinkers; our main source for the Presocratics.
vocabulary.example: Since Anaximenes’ book is lost, we rely on doxography by writers such as Theophrastus and Simplicius.

vocabulary.definition: The early Greek philosophers active before or around the time of Socrates, mostly concerned with nature and the cosmos.
vocabulary.example: The Milesians, Pythagoras, Heraclitus and Parmenides are all counted among the Presocratics.

vocabulary.definition: The view that matter is in some sense alive or ensouled throughout.
vocabulary.example: Thales’ claim that a magnet has a soul because it moves iron suggests a kind of hylozoism.

thinkingExercise.title: Be a Milesian for Fifteen Minutes
thinkingExercise.prompt: The Milesians did not have laboratories, only careful observation and bold reasoning. Try their method yourself, then try criticizing it the way each student criticized his teacher.
steps: Choose one ordinary substance (for example, fire, earth, light, or even information) and imagine you are proposing it as the arche of everything.
Write down three everyday observations that seem to support your choice, as Aristotle suggested Thales might have done with moisture and seeds.
Describe a mechanism, like Anaximenes’ rarefaction and condensation, by which your arche could turn into very different things such as rock, living bodies and air.
Now play Anaximander: write the strongest objection to your own theory. What can your substance not easily explain?
Reflect in two or three sentences: what makes a guess like this rational even when it turns out to be wrong?

summary: The Milesians searched for an arche, a single first principle underlying the variety of the world.
Thales proposed water, perhaps because life and nourishment depend on moisture; he also reportedly said all things are full of gods.
Anaximander proposed the apeiron, a boundless and indefinite source, and described nature as a lawful balance of opposites; he also argued the Earth hangs unsupported at the center.
Anaximenes proposed air and explained change mechanically through rarefaction and condensation, turning differences of quality into differences of quantity.
Their explanations were naturalistic and general, and each criticized his predecessor, creating a tradition of critical discussion that science inherits.
We know them only through later doxography, especially Aristotle, Theophrastus and Simplicius, so we must read the sources carefully.

quiz.question: What were the Milesians looking for when they asked about the arche?
options: The first king of Miletus
The single source or principle underlying all things
The god responsible for creating the world
The correct method for predicting eclipses
quiz.explanation: Arche means origin or first principle. The Milesians sought the one basic source from which everything comes and of which everything is made.

quiz.question: Which reason does Aristotle suggest Thales may have had for choosing water as the arche?
options: Water is the only substance that never changes
Miletus was built on an island
The nourishment and seeds of all things are moist
Water was sacred to Zeus
quiz.explanation: Aristotle, explicitly guessing, says Thales may have noticed that nourishment and seeds are moist, so water seemed basic to life and growth.

quiz.question: Why did Anaximander reject water as the first principle?
options: Because water is wet and cool, so it could not produce or coexist with its opposites like fire
Because water is too rare in nature
Because the gods forbade it
Because experiments showed water is made of air
quiz.explanation: If the basic stuff were one of the opposites, it could not explain the rise of its opposite and would overwhelm the others. So the source had to be indefinite: the apeiron.

quiz.question: How did Anaximander explain why the Earth does not fall?
options: It floats on an ocean of water
It rides on a cushion of air like a leaf
It is held up by the god Atlas
It sits at the center, equally distant from everything, so it has no reason to move one way rather than another
quiz.explanation: Anaximander used a symmetry argument, reported by Aristotle. Floating on water is Thales’ view, and riding on air is Anaximenes’ view.

quiz.question: Anaximenes explained differences between substances such as fire and stone as differences in how densely packed air is.
quiz.explanation: Through rarefaction and condensation, one substance (air) becomes fire when thinned and wind, cloud, water, earth and stone when compressed.

quiz.question: Why must historians treat reports about the Milesians with caution?
options: Because the Milesians wrote in a secret code
Because their own writings are lost and we rely on later authors who interpreted them through their own ideas
Because the Milesians deliberately lied about their views
Because all reports come from their enemies the Persians
quiz.explanation: We depend on doxography by Aristotle, Theophrastus and later writers like Simplicius, who may have recast earlier ideas in their own terms.

quiz.question: Thales’ reported remark that all things are full of gods shows that the Milesians completely rejected any notion of the divine.
quiz.explanation: The remark shows the opposite: Thales saw the natural world as alive and divine throughout. What was new was looking for explanations within nature rather than in myths about gods.

quiz.question: Which modern example best illustrates Anaximenes’ idea that differences in quality come from differences in quantity or arrangement?
options: A court ruling that overturns an earlier decision
A meteorologist predicting rain
Diamond and graphite both being pure carbon arranged differently
A doctor diagnosing a fever
quiz.explanation: Diamond and graphite differ hugely in appearance and hardness, yet both are carbon; the difference lies in arrangement, echoing Anaximenes’ explanation of qualities by density.

quiz.question: Anaximander’s surviving fragment describes things paying “penalty and retribution” for “injustice.” What idea does this image express?
options: Nature is governed by a lawful balance in which no opposite can dominate forever
Humans will be punished by the gods for their sins
Miletus should reform its law courts
The apeiron is a cruel and angry deity
quiz.explanation: The legal metaphor pictures opposites like hot and cold taking turns, with time restoring balance, a cosmic law rather than divine whim.

quiz.question: Anaximander’s idea that early humans developed inside fish-like creatures is essentially the same as Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection.
quiz.explanation: It was a striking naturalistic guess based on how helpless human infants are, but it had no mechanism like natural selection and no body of evidence comparable to Darwin’s.

goDeeper.body:
Should we really call the Milesians scientists? This is a live debate. In his 1958 lecture “Back to the Presocratics,” Karl Popper argued that what made the Milesians scientific was not observation but criticism. Science, for Popper, advances by bold conjectures and attempted refutations, and the Milesian school was the first to make critical discussion of a master’s theory into a tradition. Anaximander’s unsupported Earth is his star example: a theory that went far beyond, and even against, what observation suggests, since the Earth certainly looks as if it needs support. You will meet Popper properly on Day 72.

Others push back. Classicists such as G. E. R. Lloyd note that the Milesians rarely engaged in anything like systematic testing, and that “science” in our sense required later developments: mathematical modeling, deliberate experiment, and institutions for checking results. On this view the Milesians invented a style of rational speculation that later made science possible, but were not yet doing it.

There is also a question about what kind of thing the arche is. Is Thales’ water the stuff things are made of now (a material constituent), or only what they came from originally (a historical origin)? Aristotle read the Milesians as seeking his own “material cause” (Day 18), which may impose his framework on them. And the apeiron raises a puzzle that philosophers still discuss: can something with no definite properties be anything at all? This question about a featureless “stuff” underlying all qualities will return in Aristotle’s notion of prime matter and in Locke’s “something I know not what” on Day 47.

readings.note: The standard sourcebook, with original Greek, translations and commentary. Chapters 2 to 4 cover the Milesians.

readings.author: Jonathan Barnes (ed. and trans.)

readings.title: The First Scientist: Anaximander and His Legacy
readings.author: Carlo Rovelli
readings.note: A physicist’s lively argument that Anaximander launched the scientific revolution in thought.

readings.title: Conjectures and Refutations
readings.author: Karl Popper
readings.note: Contains the essay “Back to the Presocratics,” Popper’s case for the Milesians as founders of critical rationalism.

questions: Is a theory that turns out to be completely wrong still valuable if it was reasoned well? What makes it valuable?
Was Anaximenes’ return to an ordinary substance (air) a step backward from Anaximander’s apeiron, or a step forward?
Do you think there must be a single underlying stuff behind everything, or could reality be fundamentally many different kinds of things?
